listening.title: Urban Tree Watering Trials
listening.focus: Comparing effectiveness and costs of two watering methods
listening.script:
Maya: Hi Jon, have you finished reviewing the council reports for our urban forestry presentation?
Jon: Mostly. I focused on the two different watering approaches they trialled from 2021 to 2023.
Maya: Good. So the first site in North Park used deep infrequent watering – they delivered about 80 litres per tree every three weeks during summer.
Jon: Right, and the second site in Westfield used sensor-controlled drip irrigation, which released small amounts daily only when soil moisture fell below 20%.
Maya: The North Park results looked strong – 18% higher survival after two years compared to the control group with no extra watering.
Jon: Yes, but we can't take that at face value. Westfield is much hotter and has far more paved surfaces, so the trees there were already under greater stress.
Maya: The researchers acknowledged that, didn't they? They said the location difference limits any direct comparison of effectiveness.
Jon: Exactly, they qualified their conclusion and said the sensor system might have matched or even outperformed deep watering under equal conditions.
Maya: I initially thought deep watering would be cheaper, but I was wrong – the report shows labour and tanker transport made it about 15% more expensive per tree annually.
Jon: I had the same assumption. Actually, drip had higher installation costs, but after twelve months the ongoing costs dropped significantly.
Maya: What about growth measurements? I recall drip-irrigated trees had slightly smaller trunk diameters but about 10% greater canopy cover.
Jon: That's right, but the authors warned that canopy density alone doesn't necessarily indicate better long-term health without further monitoring.
Maya: So our main point should be that both methods improved survival compared to doing nothing, but the evidence for one being clearly superior remains inconclusive.
Jon: Agreed. And we should note the sample was relatively small – only 120 trees per trial – so findings should be interpreted cautiously.
Maya: Perfect. I'll prepare the slides on costs and limitations if you handle survival and growth data?

questions.title: Watering Method at North Park
questions.prompt: What did the North Park trial involve?
options: Daily drip when moisture dropped
Small amounts every day in summer
About 80 litres every three weeks
Weekly watering with tanker trucks
questions.explanation: The script states North Park delivered about 80 litres every three weeks. Option A describes the Westfield sensor method, not North Park.

questions.title: Survival Results
questions.prompt: What did the North Park results show after two years?
options: 18% higher survival than control group
18% higher survival than Westfield site
10% greater canopy cover than control
Lower survival due to paved surfaces
questions.explanation: Maya reports 18% higher survival versus the no-watering control. Option B misreads the comparison as between the two trial sites.

questions.title: Comparison Limitation
questions.prompt: Why can't the two trials be directly compared?
options: They used different tree species
Westfield had hotter, more paved conditions
North Park had smaller sample size
GPS surveys were only used at North Park
questions.explanation: Jon notes Westfield was hotter with more paved surfaces, creating greater stress. Option D invents a method difference not mentioned for these trials.

questions.title: Cost Comparison
questions.prompt: What is true about costs according to the report?
options: Deep watering had lower labour costs
Drip irrigation was cheaper to install
Both methods cost the same annually
Deep watering was about 15% more expensive yearly
questions.explanation: Maya corrects her initial view, noting labour and tanker transport made deep watering 15% more expensive annually. Option B reverses the installation cost finding.

questions.title: Growth and Overall Conclusion
questions.prompt: What do the researchers say about growth and overall findings?
options: Canopy cover alone proves better health
Both methods helped but superiority is inconclusive
Drip trees had larger trunk diameters
Sample of 120 trees was sufficient
questions.explanation: They agree both methods improved survival versus no intervention but superiority remains inconclusive, with canopy qualified as insufficient proof. Option A contradicts the authors' warning about canopy alone.

reading.title: Interpreting Uncertain Data
reading.focus: Measurement change and recruitment bias as limits on conclusions
reading.passage:
Researchers often face difficulties when data appear to show clear trends but underlying methods introduce uncertainty. Two recent studies illustrate how careful interpretation is needed before drawing firm conclusions. In both cases, the raw numbers are less informative than the conditions under which they were gathered.

The first study examined coastal erosion at Bayford over twelve years, from 2011 to 2023. Early measurements relied on aerial photographs, while from 2019 onwards the team used more precise GPS ground surveys. The combined dataset suggests the coastline retreated by an average of 0.8 metres per year, with a sharper increase to 1.4 metres per year after 2018. However, the authors emphasise that this apparent acceleration should be treated cautiously. The change in measurement technique alone could account for part of the difference, as GPS surveys detect smaller shifts that aerial images miss. In addition, two severe storms in 2020 and 2021 removed large sections of cliff in single events, temporarily inflating annual averages. When these storm years are excluded, the post-2018 rate falls to 1.0 metre per year. The authors therefore conclude that while erosion is ongoing, the exact rate of increase remains uncertain and longer monitoring with a consistent method is required. They recommend extending the GPS series for at least another five years before confirming any acceleration.

A second example comes from a student wellbeing survey conducted at a large urban university in 2023. The survey aimed to estimate overall stress levels and was distributed through social media channels and posters in the university counselling centre. Of the 420 respondents, 68% reported high levels of stress. At first glance, this figure suggests a widespread problem. The researchers, however, argue that the recruitment method likely biased the sample. Students experiencing stress may have been more motivated to participate, and those visiting the counselling centre were already seeking support. Consequently, the sample over-represented psychology undergraduates and first-year students living in university accommodation, groups known to report higher stress. The 68% figure is presented not as evidence of campus-wide prevalence, but as an illustration of how self-selection can distort results. The authors' central claim is that without random sampling, such surveys cannot reliably estimate the true proportion of highly stressed students, although they remain useful for identifying factors associated with stress among respondents. For instance, interviews with a subset of respondents revealed useful links between workload and sleep disruption, even though prevalence could not be established.

Together, these cases show that data must be read with attention to how they were collected. Recognising measurement inconsistencies and recruitment biases allows researchers to make qualified claims rather than overstating certainty. This approach strengthens credibility, even when it limits the scope of conclusions.

questions.title: Purpose of Examples
questions.prompt: Why does the author introduce the two studies?
options: To show data always misleads researchers
To illustrate need for careful interpretation
To prove coastal erosion is accelerating
To compare environmental and social methods
questions.explanation: The opening frames both studies as illustrations of careful interpretation. Option C mistakes an uncertain trend for a proven claim.

questions.title: Erosion Acceleration Uncertainty
questions.prompt: Why do authors say post-2018 acceleration is uncertain?
options: Storms removed too little cliff to measure
GPS surveys were less precise than photos
Monitoring period was only five years
Method change and storms inflated averages
questions.explanation: The passage cites technique change and two storm years as inflating the post-2018 average. Option B reverses the precision difference described.

questions.title: Conclusion on Erosion Trend
questions.prompt: What do authors conclude about Bayford erosion?
options: Erosion continues but exact increase unclear
Erosion stopped after 2021 storms
GPS data proves faster erosion now
Aerial photos underestimated earlier erosion
questions.explanation: They conclude erosion is ongoing but the rate of increase remains uncertain pending consistent monitoring. Option C overstates certainty the authors explicitly qualify.

questions.title: Meaning of 68% Figure
questions.prompt: How do researchers interpret the 68% high-stress figure?
options: Accurate estimate of campus-wide stress
Proof counselling services are ineffective
Example of distortion from self-selection
Evidence psychology students are most stressed
questions.explanation: The 68% is presented as an illustration of self-selection distortion, not prevalence. Option A is the superficial reading the authors reject.

questions.title: Value of Biased Survey
questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the wellbeing survey despite bias?
options: It can still reveal links between factors
It proves most students need counselling
It should be repeated with same method
It shows random sampling is unnecessary
questions.explanation: The authors note the survey remains useful for identifying associated factors among respondents. Option B incorrectly generalises the biased sample to all students.
